Author: @v._.v6835
Content:
One of my great-grand relatives was a worker in the palace. It was a small role, but he was old enough to pass down some stories back in the dynasties through the generations since Guangxu's period (The emperor before Puyi). It feels weird whenever I see videos like this talking about that time period, since it feels so close yet so distant.

I personally think of Puyi, along with many royalty members in the late-Qing dynasty, as a tragedy born by the system. He was elected the emperor without ever having a choice, and was thrown into different environments when the revolution happened, and again when the Japanese came. Even after the storm cleared, he was taken to be "reformed" by the government. His predecessor Guangxu suffered from similar fates, and many more people close to him as well.

Were they all good people? Certainly not. But were they given a chance to do things otherwise? Not really. These people were stuck at the end of monarchism and they never had the chance nor opportunity to adapt because of their identities.

They talked to Falun Gong practitioners who came to the body exhibition to raise awareness of human rights persecution in China and said, “We understand your concerns and support your righteous actions.” They signed the DAFOH petition to support the effort to expose forced organ harvesting.

At noon, four middle-aged people drove to the exhibition. A practitioner told them, “The exhibition organizer did not show evidence of where these bodies came from. The CCP is currently persecuting Falun Gong and other dissidents, and removing their organs while they are alive for huge profits. These corpse specimens all look like Asians. After they quietly listened, they took the materials and walked into the exhibition hall. But they soon came out.

A couple came out of the exhibition hall and were about to get in their car, when a practitioner told them that the human specimens might be from prisoners of conscience in China, and their organs might have been harvested alive. The bodies in this exhibition might be from prisoners of conscience in China. Let more people know the truth, and we can stop the persecution in China as soon as possible.”

People were deeply concerned by the cruel human rights violations. Some people suggested that citizens should call for legislation in Denmark so that such controversial exhibitions can be prevented from being held in Denmark in the future.

Author: @pineapplesareyummy6352
Content: Any Chinese in the world knows who Pu Yi is. But we also have to dispute he was ever the "most powerful kid in history". Firstly, the Imperial system was overthrown and abolished by 1911. Pu Yi never got to rule China - it was his regents who briefly controlled China, which was by then a socioeconomic and geopolitical basketcase anyway. Secondly, China is hardly the only country to have had child emperors. All monarchies with primogeniture rules, by definition, have a finite probability of children inheriting the throne. There have been child monarchs in other countries who didn't get overthrown, who grew into adults and ruled in their own right.

Author: @nv7287
Content:
Puyi had zero real power. Crowned emperor at age two, he was immediately controlled by regents, eunuchs, and Empress Dowager Longyu. Isolated in the Forbidden City, his life was strictly controlled and ritualized, with no freedom.
When Puyi ordered two eunuchs flogged and watched with delight, it wasn’t cruelty but a rare moment of agency in an otherwise powerless life. The details don’t explain if those eunuchs manipulated him, but given his isolation, it’s understandable he found relief in any small exercise of control. Later, Puyi became a puppet emperor under Japanese rule, then a Soviet captive, and finally a tool for Chinese propaganda. His entire life was defined by others’ agendas.
Calling him “the most powerful kid in history” is cruel irony. The terrified little boy hiding in a cupboard remained powerless his entire life.
Puyi did marry several times, but he never had children. His marriages were mostly arranged and deeply unhappy...
he spent nearly a decade in a communist re-education camp. When he was finally released, he was allowed to live in Beijing as an ordinary citizen.
 after his release he married a hospital worker named Li Shuxian-they had no children. Their marriage was quiet and companionable, but Puyi never experienced a typical family environment or the warmth of a family with children or a life that was free. He lived out his final years in Beijing as an ordinary citizen, working as a gardener and later as a literature researcher. He died in 1967.
He had a unique viewpoint that could have shown how both systems relied on control and shared many flaws. While no system is perfect, his experience could have revealed the similarities between imperial and communist rule in maintaining power. And that's actually a story that I would have been more interested to hear - Systems too afraid of that are too brittle to survive transparency... And the human endurance to survive..

Author: @Kstaaaaa
Content:
I think some elaboration on the Japan and China war is important: During the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945), Imperial Japan inflicted horrific atrocities on China, leaving deep scars that persist today. The invasion began after the Marco Polo Bridge Incident in 1937, leading to a full-scale war marked by extreme brutality. One of the most infamous crimes was the Nanjing Massacre (1937–1938), where Japanese troops slaughtered an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 civilians and prisoners of war in just six weeks. Soldiers carried out mass executions, bayoneted helpless victims for practice, and committed widespread rape, looting, and torture. The Japanese military also enforced the "Three Alls Policy" ("Kill All, Burn All, Loot All"), systematically destroying villages and massacring civilians to crush resistance.

Beyond conventional warfare, Japan deployed biological and chemical weapons, primarily through the notorious Unit 731, which conducted sadistic experiments on live prisoners—including vivisection, frostbite testing, and plague injections—resulting in agonizing deaths. The military also enslaved hundreds of thousands of women as "comfort women," forcing them into sexual servitude under brutal conditions. Massacres, forced labor, and scorched-earth tactics led to millions of Chinese deaths. Despite Japan’s eventual surrender in 1945, many war criminals escaped justice, and historical disputes over apologies and denial continue to strain relations. The scale of suffering inflicted by Japan during this war remains one of the darkest chapters in modern Asian history.

Author: @catcatcatcatcatcatcatcatcatca
Content:
The morals of the communist re-education in this instance are fascinating. No doubt the implementation was unethical, given the context. But western society and I personally see helping someone understand the weight of their actions is seen as a service.

Sure, ignorance is a bliss. But once one knows the weight of their own actions, few would willingly choose to return to ignorance, aside from fleeing moments of weakness.

That aspect of the re-eductation (or western justice system) is not what I would call brain washing. Even if it ”washes a brain”. If better knowledge of ones role and outcome of their choices changes them, it is still themself dictating how to adjust. Their future self with that knowledge would choose to know it, regardless of how they adjust based on the knowledge. But their past self likely has defences against learning it, meaning the process has to be persistent.

When western justice system does exactly this kind of work, we call it therapy and councelling. We have volunteers, doctors and priests specialised in it.

I am not suggesting that the cultural revolution and communist re-education is ethically comparable as an act. But in this case it is comparable as a principle.

And while it requires careful pondering, to avoid drawing false parallers and justifying the many horrors Chinese people inflicted upon itself, I do think its an eye-opening consideration: Were there people in China so privileged and removed from reality, that, according to western moral standards, it was an act of kindness to help them understand their own role and privilege, as well as the consequences of it?

One can and should still disagree with many aspects of the cultural revolution and the treatment of the people ”re-educated”. One should disagree with the overall process because those aspects, as some of the ends certainly don’t justify all of the means.

But it certainly is a viewpoint we hardly ever think: Were there landlords whose right to understand their own actions is a moral consideration in retrospect? Were some desires to re-educate the elite not zealous, but actually aligned with western ethics of enlightment?

Do child emperors deserve the kind of understanding of the institution someone working as a minimum wage museum guide possesses?
